full_text:
\> This is the 2026 version of __Joe Dolan__’s yearly Auction/Salary Cap Draft Plan, with adapted text and strategies from previous years, tailored for 2026 with specific player takes and example teams for the new season

Fantasy football auction leagues (also known as salary-cap leagues on multiple providers) feature my favorite way to draft, full stop.

There is constant action, with strategies changing on the fly. You have to pay close attention to the league around you — what other players are doing absolutely affects the way you should play. Most of all, you have to come in with a plan. That’s why I’m here to help.

Planning for an auction/salary-cap league is much less precise, though — in snake drafts, Average Draft Position (ADP) gives us a reasonable, if not bullseye-accurate, range where we can expect players to be drafted. That allows us to go into snake drafts with more specific plans than we can carry into an auction. After all, in an auction, you theoretically have a chance at *every* player. If you draw the #8 pick in your snake draft, you know you’re not getting __Bijan Robinson__. But in an auction, it doesn’t matter what nomination slot you get.

That’s what makes them so much fun to do. You’re going to end up with some *wild* roster constructions in auctions, with some teams balanced from top to bottom, others loaded up at one position but not another, and yet other teams going with massive “stars and scrubs” approaches.

Because there’s no real way to predict what the other players in your auction draft are going to do, I want this to read like my thought process when I’m going through an auction draft, which is the format I use for two of my biggest leagues of the year with my friends. I’ve had plenty of success in those leagues, and I think my plan is a pretty simple, common-sense one. If you’ve read my plan in years past, much of this article will come as no surprise. This article will be an update on my past Auction Draft Plans, with some strategies specific to the 2026 season, and others adapted from past years.

For this Auction/Salary-Cap Draft Plan, let’s assume a __12-team league with a PPR scoring system, with 1 QB, 2 RB, 2 WR, 1 TE, 2 R/W/T FLEX, 1 PK, and 1 D/ST starting__. The budget we’re working with is the standard $200. Obviously, drastically different starting lineups or league sizes will dictate different strategies (for instance, leagues that require 3 WR to start), but I thought this was the most balanced starting lineup approach to take in breaking down my plan, and it’s the format I use in my longest-running auction league (though we eliminated kickers years ago).

Before getting to Draft Day itself, let’s get into a few universal tips every auction drafter should know as they prep.

\> We have [PPR, half-PPR, and Superflex Auction Value Cheat Sheets](https://www.fantasypoints.com/nfl/downloads/season/2026/2026-auction-value-cheat-sheet) and an interactive [Auction Excel Tool](https://www.fantasypoints.com/nfl/downloads/season/2026/auction-draft-tool/2026-auction-draft-tool.xlsm)

{{CTA|DataSuite|omit=\[role\_uJb30OfZpu4pFfS7VQEq\]}}

 

### __Pre-Draft Pointers__

#### Tiers, Tiers, Tiers

I think “Tiers” drafting — grouping similarly ranked players rather than following a strict, rigid set of numerical rankings — is a good strategy to use even in a snake draft. One thing fantasy players should pound into their heads is that just because one player is ranked RB7 and another is RB8 doesn’t mean there’s a *drastic* difference between the two.

Say you’re in 10 drafts and are given the same “either/or” choice in each one. Sure, you’re drafting __Saquon Barkley__ over __TreVeyon Henderson__ 10 times out of 10 if given that choice. But what about Henderson vs. __Jaylen Warren__? Is it 7 to 3? 6 to 4? 5 to 5? They’re probably too close in your rankings to be 100% sure you’re making the right decision when you draft one. That’s because Henderson and Warren are similarly tiered on your draft sheet.

In auctions, since you have a shot at drafting any player you want, tiering them is the most important thing you can do before your draft. That’s why we “tier” [our Auction Cheat Sheet](https://www.fantasypoints.com/nfl/downloads/season/2026/2026-auction-value-cheat-sheet); although you may disagree with us and want to make adjustments (such as creating narrower tiers).

Say __Drake London__ went for $10 more than you thought he would, even though he was a target. See if you can get __Tee Higgins__ or __Nico Collins__ for a price more in line with what you were thinking.

It’s imperative to remember which tier you *must* get a player from. You may have internally decided that Tier 1 RBs are too expensive, and that’s fine. However, perhaps you also concluded that to make your plan work, you need two Tier 2 RBs. It’s essential to bid smartly but aggressively within the player tiers you need to attack.

Also, do not assume the people in your league are dumb and that you’ll be able to get away with constant values. The average fantasy player has become much smarter, and one thing I’ve noticed in every auction I’ve ever done is that the “last” player available in a perceived tier gets priced up. For instance, even though __James Cook__ might be well behind __Jonathan Taylor__ in your personal rankings, if everyone in the league perceives him as the final player available in a certain tier, don’t be shocked if he gets more money than the “better” players drafted *before* him.

__That’s why I try to get players in my targeted tiers — at least at RB and WR — while there are__ *__still players left in those tiers__*. Getting constantly caught bidding at the back end of a tier is a great way to run out of money quickly and to be “drafting from behind,” not to mention constantly drafting the last player in a tier might naturally result in a worse team — __paying a premium for an inferior product.__

When it comes to nominations, I don’t always nominate a player I want. Let’s say I’ve already drafted a top-tier RB and don’t want to double-dip, and I attacked the middle of the tier, as I suggested above. If I see one player left in that tier — let’s use the Cook example from above after all the other “RB1s” get drafted, for instance — I *love* throwing the chum into the waters and watching the sharks swarm. It creates action without me having to expend energy, and it eliminates the need for money and competition for players I *do* want at other positions or tiers.

#### Mostly, Go Cheap at QB

\> __NOTE__: This strategy focuses on 1-QB formats.

In the past decade, a gradual shift toward drafting quarterbacks earlier — and for higher prices in auction leagues — made sense given the power of [cheat-code QBs](https://www.fantasypoints.com/nfl/articles/season/2021/top-2021-konami-code-options).

Guys like 2018 __Patrick Mahomes__, 2019 __Lamar Jackson__, and 2020 __Josh Allen__ *won leagues* at barrel-bottom prices. The idea was simple: identify a mid-to-late-round QB who might be unproven or rough around the edges, but is super athletic and can add value in the run game. Profit!

{{PAYWALL}}

Eventually, the market was going to catch up to the “cheat code.” The guy we here at Fantasy Points (and, frankly, the rest of the industry) identified as that player in 2021, __Jalen Hurts__, was already priced highly (and lived up to that billing). Given that, in the last few years, I was more likely than ever to bite the bullet on an elite QB. Yes, I was paying up, but I still wanted that edge.

I’m reasonably certain I won’t have to do that this year, though I will be nominating top-tier QBs early to gauge the room's direction. *__(I especially want to see the action on Allen; more on that later.)__*

That’s not to say that Hurts, Jackson, Allen, and __Jayden Daniels__ are bad players to have on your fantasy team. Far from it! But in their markets, it will be more as an outside observer — I’ll dive in if the rest of the room is being QB-shy, but if the bids come flying in, I’ll be out.

The reason is simple.

Of the [11 quarterbacks we have projected](https://www.fantasypoints.com/nfl/projections/season/qb#/) to run for 300 or more yards, *six* are under $10 values on our Auction Cheat Sheet.

Those players are — in order of projected rushing yards — __Malik Willis__, __Jaxson Dart__, __Kyler Murray__, __Caleb Williams__, __Patrick Mahomes__, and __Justin Herbert__. Just outside 300 yards, we have __Trevor Lawrence__, __Bo Nix__, and __Tyler Shough__ all projected as affordable QBs. Consider this the “Mobile Middle Class.” *(Of this group, my favorite targets this year are Herbert, Lawrence, and Nix, in that order. We project Lawrence to be the most expensive of the three.)*

If I find the prices on the elite-tier QBs restrictive, I’m more than willing to back off and target one of these guys.

Even with more QBs providing massive upside with their legs than ever, the supply of capable but “boring” fantasy QBs — __Matthew Stafford__, __Dak Prescott__, __Brock Purdy__ — still outweighs that demand. If you want to protect your investment in your young QB, then snag one of those guys for a buck. Heck, I’d be willing to wager multiple capable fantasy QBs will even make it to your waiver wire in 1-QB formats.

Eventually, even the most aggressive QB spenders in your league (every league has the dope who has at some point drafted two elite QBs and loudly proclaimed, “I’LL JUST TRADE ONE LATER!”) will have to dedicate financial resources to filling out the rest of their rosters.

My strategy is not nearly as rigid as in years past, when I was reliably one of the last two or three players in my auction league to draft a starting QB. However, there are still numerous ways to approach the position, and it ultimately comes down to reading the room effectively early on. More on that later.

For the Cliff’s Notes version…

1. Examine the early market on __Josh Allen__ and see if there’s potential value
2. If not, pivot to targeting “the Mobile Middle Class” — especially Herbert, Lawrence, and Nix
3. If your bench has enough spots, target a “boring” veteran backup for your starter

\> *Obviously, this strategy changes drastically in 2-QB or Superflex formats, but that is not the focus of this draft plan. We do have a* [*superflex auction cheat sheet*](https://www.fantasypoints.com/nfl/downloads/season/2026/2026-auction-value-cheat-sheet)*. Ultimately, one of the “cheaper” QBs will still be a massive target for my superflex plan, either as my QB1 if I go cheap at the position, or as a high-upside QB2.*

#### Keep a Keen Eye on __Brock Bowers__

Depending on whether or not I get involved in the bidding for __Josh Allen__, I might be more willing than in years past to enter the bidding for the top TE — in this case, __Brock Bowers__. I know he had a disappointing 2025 season because of injuries and the fact that __Chip Kelly__ — one of the biggest charlatans in NFL history — was calling the offense for much of the year, but I think Bowers has absolute league-breaking upside this year with better health, better QB play, and a competent coach.

 "A football robot from heaven." That's what Klint Kubiak called Brock Bowers #Raiders #FantasyFootball Is Bowers a lock for TE1 in 2026? ➡️ https://t.co/dvKAlqnzIR @GrahamBarfield @Fantasy_Guru pic.twitter.com/K40zQAnvHa — Fantasy Points (@FantasyPts) July 10, 2026 

Again, if I’ve already spent up for Allen, I’m not likely to enter the bidding for Bowers (or vice versa). But I think Bowers is so far above even __Trey McBride__ this year that having him on my team is uniquely appealing.

If I don’t get Bowers, I’m out on McBride at his projected cost. But I am willing to examine the market for second-year studs __Colston Loveland__ and __Tyler Warren__. If those two guys get too heavy into the $20s, then I’m going dumpster diving. A key player in that regard is __Tucker Kraft__, who is coming off a serious knee injury but was tied with McBride as the TE1 in FPG before he went down. The same applies to __George Kittle__, though I’m skeptical that he’s as far along in his recovery from his January Achilles injury as he says he is. Still, it’s hard to argue against Kittle’s upside case.

If I draft Bowers, Loveland, or Warren (or McBride, if you’re into that), I’m not drafting a second TE. If I grab my pivot in Kraft (or Kittle), I’m probably going to get a $1 “catch the ball and fall down” type like __Dalton Schultz__ to give me a floor play if it takes Kraft (or Kittle) time to get their legs under them.

If your league has one TE spot and isn’t TE premium (i.e., 1.5 PPR for TEs, [like the FFPC](https://myffpc.com/cms/public/?affid=fantasypoints)), I think it’s only worth getting into a bidding war for a *true* difference-maker, like Bowers.

__Like at QB, this is all personal preference. If you don’t want to spend up for an elite option… don’t! There are plenty of great ways to build a team in an auction.__

#### Only Enter Serious Bidding Wars if You’re OK Drafting the Player

It’s extremely frustrating to sit back in an auction and watch your competition select players for a value you think is way too low.

Say you placed a $15 value on __Jalen Hurts__, and it looks like he’s about to go off the board for only $8. Meanwhile, you just spent $29 on __Josh Allen__. *Ugh*. You’d much rather have Hurts at $8, and $21 extra to spend elsewhere!

Because you’re frustrated, you put in a $9 bid on Hurts — *there is no way you’re letting him go cheap*. Your opponent counters quickly, entering a $10 bid. *Well, he’s willing to go higher…* so you click the bid button to raise it to $11.

And then… silence. *You misread the room*. No one else bids, and you’re stuck with Hurts at a “value”… but at a position you didn’t need. You have a great fantasy QB, yes, but you already had one, and now you have $18 fewer to fill out your roster. And now, you’re accidentally the doofus I referenced earlier — you’re stuck with two elite QBs but can only play one, and you're likely going to be eating up a bench spot, making impossible decisions every week, *or* being forced to take nickels on the dollar back in a trade. None of those are optimal outcomes.

Handcuffing *yourself* in an auction draft is the most common and easiest way to lose. It’s also the easiest to avoid. It’s better to let your opponent get value than to cripple your ability to get a good player at a fair cost later.

#### Do Not Spend More than $1 on a PK or D/ST

Don’t do it. Just don’t.

As dull as it is, some folks will throw out a kicker and/or defense early in a draft. It fills roster spots and provides cost certainty (most auction software calculates your total remaining budget, as well as the average and maximum bids you can spend on a player). The idea is this — if you get your targeted kicker for $1, great! If some moron in my league decided to bid that kicker up to $2 or $3, that’s a few bucks they can’t spend later.

Even if you *really want* __Brandon Aubrey__, *do not get in a bidding war for a kicker!* It is not worth it! You’ll see the rewards late in the draft when you have that extra dollar or two to guarantee you get that final sleeper to round out your bench.

(I’ll talk about an opposite kicker/defense strategy later, one I picked up from my guy __Drew Davenport__. It involves waiting until the last couple of rounds to nominate one, and it makes a lot of sense given how tense the last rounds of nomination are.)

#### Know Your Software

Obviously, knowing how to work the auction/salary-cap software at Yahoo!, ESPN, or wherever you plan to play is critical to doing a successful auction/salary-cap draft. However, you should also research the projected and average values offered by those software platforms. In many leagues, especially early in the draft, fantasy drafters won’t stray too far from them. That can give you a leg up on identifying values even before your draft.

\> Here are [Yahoo!’s projected values](https://football.fantasysports.yahoo.com/f1/draftanalysis?type=salcap) and [ESPN’s projected values](https://fantasy.espn.com/football/livedraftresults).

#### Make Sure Everyone is at the Draft

This isn’t so much a “pointer” as it is a quality-of-life tip. There is absolutely nothing worse than an auction with an auto-draft team. Why? Most auction/salary-cap software will automatically draft a team by having that player bid up to the software’s recommended auction value. It will often bid up to the value, not a dollar more or less.

You, and multiple other teams in your league, could be executing a strategy perfectly. You could have an excellent value lined up at the position and tier you targeted. You could be slated to land a player for $10 fewer than you expected. And when the clock is ticking away on the nomination… the autodraft team chimes in.

Make no mistake: the autodraft team is going to *suck out loud*. It will pay a premium for both the QB and TE positions. It might bid up a kicker or a defense. It doesn’t have the intelligence to know when it’s prudent to go *above* projected value (e.g. at the end of a tier), leaving the team shorthanded. But it will also take a lot of the fun and strategy out of your room. It will ruin the organic experience that makes auctions the most fun way to draft.

If someone can’t make your auction and rescheduling isn’t an option, have that person find someone to draft for them, or replace the team. It’s that simple.

### __On Draft Day__

#### At the Beginning of Your Draft (First Three Rounds)

Consider this your plan for the first three rounds of nominations for your draft. This is where the *elite* players are going to go. Just like a snake draft, it’s probably going to be unbalanced — the first three rounds of nominations will carry much more weight than the next three, though in auctions, some players can slip through the cracks.

This is where you want to be “selectively aggressive.” I’d like to leave this portion of the draft with at *least* two high-level players I feel good about, but I don’t want to go nuts here and leave my bankroll short for the crucial middle rounds. However, if I leave *all my money* for the middle rounds, I will have a very deep but dreadfully mediocre team.

The first thing I will do is watch the rest of the room. I want to see if players are being ridiculously aggressive (bidding __Bijan Robinson__ up to $75, for example), or are being sheepish. Even in an auction, when *any player can be nominated at any point*, there will be at least a handful of elite-level players nominated early.

If the bidding for the Robinsons, McCaffreys, and Gibbses of the world is approaching 35% of the total team budgets, I will probably sit back and watch the money drain out of the rest of the league and start targeting Tier-Two RBs. If I find the bidding reasonable, I’ll be in on the action. *It’s up to you to decide where you’re comfortable*, and I can’t predict how your specific room will react. That’s what makes auctions fun, but also what makes this article inexact!

Secondly, here’s that __Josh Allen__ strategy I was referring to earlier. Amidst a lot of [consternation about personnel shifts, the death of fantasy WR2s](https://www.fantasypoints.com/nfl/articles/2025/ryan-heaths-fantasy-football-takeaways#/), and all the challenges to what we thought we knew about fantasy football over the last decade… what if the answer is to just draft __Josh Allen__?

I admit this is a kick to my stomach to consider given how I typically want to draft the QB position, but [Scott Barrett wrote this earlier this offseason](https://www.fantasypoints.com/nfl/articles/2026/brain-trust-favorite-best-ball-pick), and it got me thinking quite a bit. It was geared toward winning a large-field best-ball tournament, but let’s try to apply that to our auction format:

*“Ask your favorite best ball bro what their Josh Allen exposure is. If Josh Allen isn’t one of their top-3 highest-owned QBs, I’m not sure they know what they’re doing. He’s easily the biggest edge pick at the QB position, which is the position that scores the most fantasy points. That becomes crucially important as you need to advance through each round of the tournament to have a chance at the $2M grand prize.*

*Sure, Allen’s safety, consistency, floor, and median are all great — he’s finished (counting backward) as the QB1, QB2, QB1, QB2, QB1, and QB1 by FPG over the last six fantasy seasons. But that almost pales in comparison to his legitimately unrivaled weekly ceiling — he averages 41.7 FPG over his seven best games over the last three seasons (versus Lamar Jackson’s 34.2 or Patrick Mahomes’ 29.4). He needs to have one of those games only once during the tournament rounds to be a ‘nearly impossible to advance without player’ And that’s the main point — the only players who offer similar ‘impossible to win the tournament without them’ upside are being drafted in Round 1, and Allen is going late-Round 3/early-Round 4.*

*But another bonus of drafting Allen is that he also gives you an extra roster spot, because you probably don’t need a QB3 if Allen is who he’s been over the last six years.”*

Again, Scott wasn’t thinking about optimal redraft/managed roster-building with this take. He is trying to find an edge in a format where swinging for the fences is *necessary*. So that’s an important caveat. But to build on his point… my auction value cheat sheet has Allen as, roughly, a $30 player. It has __Jahmyr Gibbs__ as a *$70* player. And Scott already outlined Allen’s unique floor *and* ceiling… at a position that is historically more durable than RB or WR. Moreover, there’s no need to draft a backup QB. Just keep that open roster spot for another position and go waiver hunting when Allen is on bye (Week 7).

When I’m nominating in this early stage of the draft, I want to keep that in mind. You can rest assured that one of my nominations early will be Allen, provided someone else hasn’t already nominated him. I’m doing this because I *want* Allen (or, on the cheaper end, __Lamar Jackson__), even if I plan to live in the “Mobile Middle Class.” I’ve been in enough auctions where bidders are playing chicken at the QB position. If I’m able to come in underneath my projected value for Allen, I will be willing to write the check.

Now, building your auction team exclusively on “values” is a good way to suck in an auction league (and in most leagues). At most positions, you get what you pay for. But I throw that rule completely out the window when I’m drafting my quarterback in a 1-QB auction league. I *will* get value at this position, and you will too. __It is a GUARANTEE__. It’s just a matter of whether that value comes from an elite QB like Allen or a rock-solid starter. Let me explain.

If you’re drafting with a bunch of sharps who generally understand that late-round (or late-auction) QB strategies work, they’ll be less likely to pay up for the elite QBs like Allen. If so, *I will take a value on the game-changing QB.* But I only want one of them *if I can get a value* — say, $21 when I have a $30 projected value on the player. Why? Even in this new era of fantasy football, in which the mobile quarterback is more important than it was 10 years ago, *the supply of capable fantasy QBs still exceeds demand*.

__Matthew Stafford__ and __Jordan Love__, for example, aren’t going to go for more than a buck or two in *any* 1-QB salary-cap draft, even one in which Allen and Jackson go for $30-35. __The high-end QB market being blown out of proportion__ *__will not affect the lower end__*__.__ Trickle-down economics simply do not work in 1-QB salary-cap leagues. So if my leaguemates want to spend $25-30 on the elite QBs, I’ll be bottom-feeding later in the draft. If they don’t, I’ll buy into the upper class.

Moving on, this is the draft area in which you’ll almost certainly be interested in most of the players who go up for nomination, since most of your room will nominate the best players. When I’m nominating and bidding at this stage of the draft, I’m going to start with a competitive bid. *There is no reason to nominate* *__Ja’Marr Chase__* *at $1 when there’s no chance he’s going for that little!* Nominate a player at this stage of a draft for at least 40% of his projected cost (for instance, if Chase’s projected value is $50, start with a bid of at least $20). This will help your draft move along quicker, and it’ll be a more pleasant experience for all involved. It’ll also get only the serious bidders to bite, which speeds things up as well.

When I’m bidding on an early-round player I really want, I try to be “stealthy.” That doesn’t mean I wait until the final second to bid that extra dollar, but I try to let most of the bidding get done before I wade into the waters. An elite player will always get a flurry of activity very quickly. Once that activity starts to slow down a little bit, that’s when I might pop in my bid. I don’t want to make it blatantly obvious that I *really want a player*, because that could encourage someone else in my league to bid that player up. In some ways, it’s almost like betting in poker. You have to be assertive, but not obvious. You want players to wonder what you’re doing, not feel as if they can exploit your strategy. This is another reason I like to get my players before a tier dries up — I don’t want my leaguemates to look at my roster and bids and think I’m desperate, which would expose me to bid-ups.

After I get a player in the early rounds, I typically sit back and wait for a couple of nominations to see where the room is going and for more money to clear out. There are enough high-quality players to go around at this stage, so I won’t feel terribly left out if another team grabs someone I had my eye on. But I’m still paying attention because I *will* get involved if a player gets underbid.

Still, *__you do not need to be involved in the bidding for every player!__* There is no worse feeling in an auction than trying to encourage a “bidding war” on a player you didn’t want, only to get saddled with them and destroy your budget in the process, as mentioned earlier. If you don’t want a player, I wouldn’t go past bidding 70% or so of that player’s projected value, even if it’s a “bargain.” (For instance, if you wanted nothing to do with __Ashton Jeanty__ this year, even getting him for $35 of a projected $48 salary on Yahoo! — a “bargain” — takes $35 away from your budget to target someone you actually wanted.)

This can especially be a big mistake if you’ve already spent up on a position like QB (Allen) or TE (__Brock Bowers__, for whom the Allen strategy also applies), where you only need to start one and get saddled with an expensive backup at a position you don’t need. It’s the most avoidable but most crippling mistake one can make in an auction.

Two more things about these early rounds…

While this is a range where you’re likely interested in most of the players, I also might use this opportunity to throw up elite-tier players if I’m not interested in that particular cost, like if I had a predraft strategy to avoid paying the premium for __Christian McCaffrey__. This sucks money out of the draft and gives me more resources to attack the tiers I want to draft from.

In this range, you might see your leaguemates nominate a kicker or defense alongside some elite players. There are a few reasons for that. For one, the auction software you’re using likely calculates both your maximum and average remaining bids. Since you shouldn’t pay more than $1 for a kicker or defense, this provides a more accurate representation of the money you have left per player. Secondly, if anyone in the league wants to bid up a kicker or a defense, *that’s fine and dandy*. You’ll be surprised later in your draft how much that extra dollar or two will come in handy (more on that later… along with a PK/DST strategy I prefer late in drafts).

It’s worth noting that [our auction values](https://www.fantasypoints.com/nfl/rankings/auction/qb?season=2026) suggest big-money *running backs* might actually be underpriced compared to your expectations given recent trends, but there’s no real way for me to predict how your room will react. This is why you have to stay on your feet.

In this range of the draft (not counting whether I select a PK or D/ST), I probably want to secure my roster with 3 great-to-rock-solid players at RB and WR, or 2 and either __Josh Allen__ or __Brock Bowers__ if the price is right.

*As a player-specific take,* *__Tee Higgins__* *is a player I really like who makes multiple builds possible.* I think he can produce like a fantasy WR1 at a fantasy WR2 cost, and an early nomination of Higgins isn’t likely to invite the flurry of bids like it would for his teammate __Ja’Marr Chase__. If I can land Higgins for my projected $24 value (or, honestly, even a little bit more), that will open me to bidding at the top end of the RB market for a Bijan or Gibbs.

Ultimately, I want to leave the first three rounds of nominations with between 40-60% ($80-120 in a $200 cap) of my budget remaining. That might sound like a lot to spend on just a handful of players, but it’ll become obvious soon that players will become drastically more affordable… and that’s where you win your draft.

#### In the Middle of Your Draft

This will be the biggest part of the draft, somewhere between 10-12 rounds of nominations. And this is where the majority of your team will be constructed (presuming, of course, you didn’t go “Stars-N-Scrubs” and need to wait an impossibly long time to fill out your roster). There are some really great options to fill out your roster in this range. Some include RBs __David Montgomery__ and __Javonte Williams__; plus WRs __DeVonta Smith__, __Christian Watson__, __Jameson Williams__, and __Parker Washington__.

In this part of your draft, you need to pay attention to several things. First of all, keep an eye on __“The Hammer”__ — this is the term I use for the drafter with the most money left. This player can throw around weight to get a target, which can be problematic if that player is the last in a tier.

But in addition to keeping watch on The Hammer, you need to know the construction of the other rosters in the league. That’s because, even if you execute your plan flawlessly, you’re going to run into some competition for players. If you need a wide receiver and you notice that three teams with more money than you *also* need a wide receiver, you had better get on that sooner rather than later because, again, *you do not want to get caught in a bidding war at the end of a tier*, especially with someone who has more money than you.

This is also the part of my draft where I will strategically nominate *players I don’t want*. It’s a wonderful exercise to enter an auction draft with 10-15 players you’d rather pass on (I touched on this in the last section). But you might also add players to that list during the draft. Perhaps I got someone like __Brock Bowers__ a few rounds of nominations in. If __Tyler Warren__ is still on the board, I may nominate him at a low price to encourage a bidding war and get some money out of the room (but again, *don’t get in a bidding war for a player you don’t need to try to get extra money out of someone*). If a big-named player I’m out on — someone like __Malik Nabers__, just for an example — has slipped through the cracks and still hasn’t been nominated, I’m giddy to throw him to the wolves and watch from a safe distance.

Another “bidding war” tip: *__don’t get into a bidding war for someone way down the draft board, even if it’s a guy you’re targeting!__* Here’s an example. Say you’re in on Buccaneers RB __Kenneth Gainwell__ as one of your big sleepers. I like him, too — he’s [RB31 on our Auction Cheat Sheet](https://www.fantasypoints.com/nfl/downloads/season/2026/2026-auction-value-cheat-sheet). But there are still several Tier 2 and Tier 3 RBs available, guys you objectively have to like more Gainwell.

If Gainwell is nominated, it’s OK to put in a bid, but *resist going way over the top to land him*. You will be *shocked* by how many players in useful categories — the hot young breakout candidate or reliable overlooked veteran — will fall to the end stages of your draft and will be available for much less. In fact, if I’m in a league of sharper players, I might look to nominate a popular breakout candidate early to try to get overpays.

My goal in this section is to “wax and wane” — that is, float between having “The Hammer” for myself (while not being afraid to use it) and falling to the bottom of the league in terms of available budget for a little bit. While you don’t necessarily want to get caught spending $30 on a player you had valued at $15 because he’s the last start-worthy RB left, you *also* shouldn't be afraid to spend $5 or so extra to get the Tier-3 player you need. As I said earlier, I want to try to be “stealthy” and not make it obvious that I really want a player. An early flurry of bidding activity could encourage less plugged-in players to get involved and push the price up. (*“Oh crap, the whole league wants this guy, I should go get him!”*)

There’s a balance between spending way too much to land that hot sleeper and going over the top to land an end-of-tier difference-maker. The worst thing you can do at an auction is keep a significant portion of your budget in your pocket. I think anything more than $5 left over from a $200 cap is criminal, and the only person you’re robbing is yourself. Believe me, this is the range where spending a couple of bucks over your projected value is fine — there is a big difference between bidding aggressively on a difference-maker and bidding stupidly just to land that sleeper you must have.

*__If you sit back and wait for values to fall into your lap, your team will suck__*__.__ Sure, you might get a value or two that really help you open up your wallet for other players, but “hope” is not a strategy.

If you haven’t yet drafted your starting QB, this is where you do it — ideally toward the back end of this stage. I typically don’t like to spend more than $5 if I’m grabbing a non-elite QB — this might be where I draft __Justin Herbert__ or __Bo Nix__. You can even add a solid QB2 to the equation for $1-3 and spend a fraction of what __Josh Allen__ went for.

The meat of your draft ends when you have three or four roster spots remaining. Somewhere between 5-10% ($10-20 in a $200 cap) of your budget left for the stretch run should be the goal.

#### At the End of Your Draft

Once you reach this part of the draft, you should identify the player you *must* have on the end of the roster. And pay to go get him… provided you have the capital to do so.

Here’s why it’s so important to have those few extra bucks lying around from not paying up for a PK or D/ST. There are going to be plenty of players nominated here who are “projected” to go for $1-2 on your cheat sheet or by the auction software, but the reality is the most appealing players in this tier go for significantly more than that because everyone with money left is going to spend up to get the late-round guys they want.

Nominations and bids can get tricky here. __Remember: EVERY PLAYER WHO GOES UP FOR NOMINATION GETS DRAFTED. And if no one bids on the player you nominated, YOU GET THAT PLAYER.__ That might sound self-evident, but let me explain further.

If you think the rest of your league has the same sleeper or two in mind as you do, you might think to avoid nominating him so you have a better chance of landing him. *However*, if you try to get cute and nominate a scrub, the rest of the league may call your bluff, and you'll end up with a $1 jabroni you didn’t want! You can’t un-nominate a player just because you didn’t get any bites on your lure.

Why is this important? Because not only is your budget finite, *but so are your roster spots*. __There are two kinds of currency in an auction draft!__

If you fill a 16-man roster but still have $15 left on your budget, you don’t get that $15 back. You don’t get to create an extra roster spot to use that $15 on. And you’ll make yourself sick looking at the WR3s you could have scored for that $15 in hindsight, or the late-round “sleepers” on whom you could have spread that money around. I don’t know about your league, but I’ve never been in one where the person with the most money left over after the draft got rewarded.

This is where saving your kicker and defense nominations may come in handy if you didn’t pick one up earlier! Paraphrasing __Drew Davenport__ here — if you have those bullets left in your chamber, it can buy you time in your nominations to wait around for the real sleepers you want, and to wait for some money to clear out of the room. I’m never going to be upset if someone outbids me for a kicker or defense, and that’s one fewer roster slot in the league for the players I want.

Along the same lines, this is yet another stage where it’s cognizant to be aware of “The Hammer.” If you have it, *use it*. It’s not the time to be patient with it like you might have been in the middle rounds. Don’t get into cutesy bidding wars — if there’s a player you want, go get him. If you *don’t* have it, try to keep an eye on which position “The Hammer” might be eyeing.

Every year, there are millions of reports about low-end players you might not even be thinking about now whom you might want to draft in early September. The sleeper you’re convinced you’re *really* going to slip through the cracks and get for $1? Chances are, others in your league think the exact same thing.

That leads me to another late-round auction point: *__never get caught in a position where you can’t make your maximum bid on a player you really want__*. So not only do you want to be aware of “The Hammer” and how much he can spend, but you also want to know everyone’s maximum bid and how many roster spots they have left.

Here’s an example. Say you now have two roster spots left and $4 to spend. You really want Packers TE __Tucker Kraft__, because you opted not to pay up for a top-tier TE. Your league-mate, who has $3 left to spend on one roster spot, nominates Kraft for $1. You immediately top the bid with a bump to $2… but your opponent, who has $3 left, is able to top *that* bid. Even though you had $4 left, you put yourself in a position where you couldn’t top a $3 bid because you needed to fill two roster spots and must have $1 left over to do so.

What should you have done? If you’re down to your last two or three roster spots and *really want a certain player*, immediately put in your maximum bid. If someone can top it, then so be it. But making a simple accounting mistake like outlined above is a titanic bummer.

### __Example Teams__

I was hesitant to do this since auctions are extremely fluid, and values really do move up and down during a draft (which our [Auction Excel Tool](https://www.fantasypoints.com/nfl/downloads/season/2026/auction-draft-tool/2026-auction-draft-tool.xlsm) accounts for). If spending is out of control early in your draft and players are going for significantly more than you expected, then the middle rounds will be full of players going for less than their projected values.

But assuming sane drafting — rarely a safe assumption — let’s examine what ideal teams would look like, using ranges from our [Auction Values Cheat Sheet](https://www.fantasypoints.com/nfl/downloads/season/2026/2026-auction-value-cheat-sheet).

\> This is a 12-team, $200 budget PPR league with 1 QB, 2 RB, 2 WR, 1 TE, 2 R/W/T FLEX, 1 PK, and 1 D/ST starting and 6 bench spots (16 spots total).

#### The Balanced Approach

QB: __Justin Herbert__ ($6), __Bo Nix__ ($2)

RB: __Jonathan Taylor__ ($59), __David Montgomery__ ($22), __Jaylen Warren__ ($10), __Rachaad White__ ($5), __Dylan Sampson__ ($1)

WR: __CeeDee Lamb__ ($41), __Tee Higgins__ ($26), __Parker Washington__ ($11), __Jayden Reed__ ($5), __Quentin Johnston__ ($1), __Tre Tucker__ ($1)

TE: __Sam LaPorta__ ($8)

PK: __Jake Bates__ ($1)

D/ST: __Jacksonville Jaguars__ ($1)

\> *On a balanced team, I’d allocate 5-10% of my budget for each of QBs and TEs, 35-45% for each of RBs and WRs, and 1% for kickers plus defenses.*

My goal with this team was to get a #1 at each position I felt very good about, while not skimping as much on depth. I have a strong RB2 in __David Montgomery__, a QB/WR team stack, and if Addison or Reed hits as my WR3, this team is going places. However, you can see how just one injury to a stud could really set this team back if one of the guys I’m betting on for upside — Warren, Johnston — doesn’t come through.

This is a viable strategy for sure, though, especially if you’re willing to drop down $10 or so to a guy like __James Cook__ as a #1 RB, giving yourself more money to spend for WR or RB depth… or to pay up for a guy like __Colston Loveland__ at TE.

Most auction drafters, especially those just beginning, will try to accomplish this strategy. It’s harder than you might think, because you really need to be disciplined with your tiers.

#### RB-Leaning

QB: __Jaxson Dart__ ($4), __Matthew Stafford__ ($2)

RB: __Saquon Barkley__ ($45), __Jeremiyah Love__ ($33), __D’Andre Swift__ ($16), __Kenny Gainwell__ ($4), __Aaron Jones__ ($3)

WR: __George Pickens__ ($28), __Zay Flowers__ ($23), __Ladd McConkey__ ($16), __Mike Evans__ ($13), __Wan’Dale Robinson__ ($4)

TE: __Harold Fannin__ ($6), __Dalton Schultz__ ($1)

PK: __Tyler Bass__ ($1)

D/ST: __Minnesota Vikings__ ($1)

\> *On an RB-leaning team, I’d allocate 3-5% of my budget for each of QBs and TEs, roughly 50-55% for RBs, 35-40% for WRs, and 1% for kickers plus defenses.*

On this team, I didn’t spend up at either QB or TE. I really got some depth at WR, where the values are. My RBs are top-heavy but have some incredible upside (and potential trade bait) if Gainwell snags a big role. But there’s a risk Love is hurt by being on a bad team that forces a committee backfield, or the Eagles’ offense doesn’t make the expected improvements and Saquon doesn’t come close to regaining his 2024 form.

I have to acknowledge that this kind of build was *ideal* in 2024 and 2025 — last year’s version of this build had __Derrick Henry__, __Chase Brown__, __Trevor Lawrence__, *and* __Jaxon Smith-Njigba__ on it. Good luck beating that team in the fantasy playoffs last year!

I’ll have a comfortable amount of depth, especially at RB, but WR is pretty thin if I take a bearish view. Pickens is a flight risk; Flowers is in a new offense; McConkey was a one-year wonder in 2024; Evans gets his powers sapped by the Santa Clara substation. You can make a compelling case for *all* those individuals, but it’s essential to consider the range of potential outcomes when assembling a team like this.

#### WR-Leaning

QB: __Jaxson Dart__ ($4), __Matthew Stafford__ ($2)

RB: __Breece Hall__ ($27), __Cam Skattebo__ ($21), __Chuba Hubbard__ ($14), __Rico Dowdle__ ($7), __Blake Corum__ ($1)

WR: __Amon-Ra St. Brown__ ($45), __Drake London__ ($34), __DeVonta Smith__ ($21), __Parker Washington__ ($10), __Jordyn Tyson__ ($3), __Jayden Higgins__ ($1)

TE: __Kyle Pitts__ ($9)

PK: __Eddy Pineiro__ ($1)

D/ST: __Philadelphia Eagles__ ($1)

\> *On a WR-leaning team, I’d allocate 3-5% of my budget for each of QBs and TEs, roughly 35-40% for RBs, 50-55% for WRs, and 1% for kickers plus defenses.*

This is the same QB group as the team above… but with the RB and WR strategies flipped. I have to admit, in years past I’d much prefer this kind of build, but I’m scared to death of this RB group this year. It seems like the markets are pricing the RBs appropriately with this build.

Hall is on a bad team and his coach continues to talk of a committee; Skattebo is coming off a bad injury; Hubbard is coming off a bad season. It’s easy to see where this could go wrong. However, if *one* of those RBs hits, the WRs should be enough to carry this team to contention.

#### RB-Heavy (RB-Robust)

QB: __Brock Purdy__ ($5), __Tyler Shough__ ($1)

RB: __Bijan Robinson__ ($67), __Ashton Jeanty__ ($40), __David Montgomery__ ($20), __Kenny Gainwell__ ($4)

WR: __Terry McLaurin__ ($15), __Jameson Williams__ ($14), __Christian Watson__ ($10), __Michael Pittman__ ($8), __Carnell Tate__ ($5), __Rashid Shaheed__ ($1)

TE: __Dallas Goedert__ ($7), __Isaiah Likely__ ($1)

PK: __Cameron Dicker__ ($1)

D/ST: __Houston Texans__ ($1)

\> *On an RB-robust team, I’d allocate 2-4% of my budget for each of QBs and TEs, 65-75% for RBs, 25-30% for WRs, and 1% for kickers plus defenses.*

In order to fit three high-priced RBs into my budget, I had to load up on WR3s and low-dollar values at QB and TE. This is a more fragile approach than I’d recommend, but if some combo of these highly volatile receivers hits near its ceiling, I could be in business. That actually happened last year — I recommended both __Zay Flowers__ and __George Pickens__ in this section last year. The *problem* is that, while i had __Jahmyr Gibbs__ on last year’s team, my #2 RB was a $40 __Bucky Irving__. YIKES.

Obviously, you can win with this kind of team, but I don’t think it’s for me, given historical injury rates at RB *vis-a-vis* WR (I still believe the last two years to be outliers).

#### Zero-RB

QB: __Josh Allen__ ($30)

RB: __Chuba Hubbard__ ($14), __Jaylen Warren__ ($10), __Jadarian Price__ ($8), __Kenny Gainwell__ ($4), __Kyle Monangai__ ($2), __Blake Corum__ ($1)

WR: __Ja’Marr Chase__ ($55), __Rashee Rice__ ($31), __Tee Higgins__ ($22), __Jakobi Meyers__ ($11), __Matthew Golden__ ($1)

TE: __Harold Fannin__ ($8), __Chig Okonkwo__ ($1)

PK: __Jason Myers__ ($1)

D/ST: __Green Bay Packers__ ($1)

\> *On a Zero-RB team, I’d allocate 15-30% for QBs plus TEs (spending big at one or both positions), 20-25% for RBs, 45-65% for WRs, and 1% for kickers plus defenses.*

My entire RB corps for this group cost $39… or *$28 fewer than I spent on* *__Bijan Robinson__* *alone on the last team*. The money saved from going Zero-RB went to an elite QB and a loaded receiving corps — and obviously, the presumption is I’ll be using my sick WR group to fill my two FLEX spots.

You can also see how the same would work if you want to pivot away from __Josh Allen__ and instead spend that money on __Brock Bowers__ — say, $37 for Bowers and two one-dollar fliers at QB. Easily adaptable

This team needs one of these RBs to hit the big time. *Maybe* Hubbard’s entire season last year was derailed by injury. *Maybe* Warren thrives with __Kenny Gainwell__ gone. *Maybe* the Seahawks commit to Price as a rookie. *Maybe* Gainwell continues to be a coaches’ pet with a new team. *Maybe* Corum becomes a league winner if __Kyren Williams__ goes down. If just one hits, I can put everything else together by mixing and matching my RB2 for the rest of the year. But if that happens…. well, you see the appeal of Zero RB.

I will have you know that my longest-running auction league — the basis for this article — was won with a Zero-RB strategy five years ago (2021)… by yours truly! What’s the key to that? Well… just like in any other league, it’s drafting the right players and working the Waiver Wire. I got __Leonard Fournette__ for $5, and he was a bell cow all season. I used fantastic playoff-week performances from __Justin Jackson__ and __Boston Scott__ (both acquired off waivers) to cover for Fournette’s injury. I also spent $12 on __Damien Harris__, and he had 15 rushing TDs. Saving money on RBs allowed me to spend up at TE, where __Mark Andrews__ was my team MVP.

In fact, this strategy worked so well for me that I was able to overcome spending $48 on __Calvin Ridley__ the year he stepped away from football.

Was some of it good luck? Of course. But I drafted so many RBs with theoretical upside that I was able to get a couple to hit — my most expensive RB was __Javonte Williams__, and while he certainly was solid as a rookie, he wasn’t the best of the bunch.

__While I will always have a place in my heart for Zero-RB builds, I think it’s become a lot harder to execute. So how about modifying that strategy just a bit in my next build?__

#### “Hero RB”

QB: __Jayden Daniels__ ($13)

RB: __Christian McCaffrey__ ($53), __TreVeyon Henderson__ ($12), __Rico Dowdle__ ($8), __Rachaad White__ ($2), __Jonathon Brooks__ ($1)

WR: __Amon-Ra St. Brown__ ($33), __Mike Evans__ ($25), __DeVonta Smith__ ($17), __Josh Downs__ ($10), __Jauan Jennings__ ($6), __Rashod Bateman__ ($1)

TE: __Tucker Kraft__ ($7), __Dalton Schultz__ ($1)

PK: __Chris Boswell__ ($1)

D/ST: __Denver Broncos__ ($1)

\> *On a “Hero-RB” team, I’d allocate 2-35% of my budget to one RB… and then 10-15% on the rest of my RBs combined. I’d want to spend no more than about 45% of my budget on the RB position, even including the “Hero RB.” I’d then try to get my QB and TEs for 10-20% of my budget, and the rest allocated to WRs (35-50%).*

“Hero RB,” or “Modified Zero RB,” involves drafting one high-priced RB and attempting to “stream” RB2 the rest of the way.

The appeal is evident. Not only did I land a super-stud in CMC, but I was also able to get a higher-priced QB in Daniels and still have a balanced and deep WR corps.

I didn’t have to go dumpster-diving at TE either, getting a player I really like in Kraft. If one of Henderson, Dowdle, White, or Brooks hits even low-end RB2/high-end RB3 value, this team is cooking with grease… *if* CMC stays on the field. And if he doesn’t? Well, see you next year.

#### “Stars-N-Scrubs”

QB: __Drake Maye__ ($15)

RB: __Bijan Robinson__ ($65), __Kenny Gainwell__ ($5), __Blake Corum__ ($1), __Jonathon Brooks__ ($1), __Chris Rodriguez__ ($1)

WR: __Jaxson Smith-Njigba__ ($50), __Jaylen Waddle__ ($12), __Jordyn Tyson__ ($3), __Wan’Dale Robinson__ ($2), __Makai Lemon__ ($1), __Quentin Johnston__ ($1), __Stefon Diggs__ ($1)

TE: __Brock Bowers__ ($40)

PK: __Ka’imi Fairbairn__ ($1)

D/ST: __Los Angeles Rams__ ($1)

The top four players on this roster cost me $170 of a $200 budget — leaving me $30 to fill out the rest of my roster, and 12 spots to fill. Whew. For this to work with a Bowers buy, I had to eschew a true “stud” QB and go more upper-mid-tier with Maye as opposed to spending for __Josh Allen__ or __Lamar Jackson.__

Stars-N-Scrubs is a hyper-fragile strategy, it goes without saying. If you spend this kind of money, one injury means your team goes up in flames (hello, __Christian McCaffrey__ in 2021/2024, __Jonathan Taylor__ in 2022, __Austin Ekeler__ in 2023, and __Malik Nabers__ in 2025).

It is possible for Stars-N-Scrubs to work… if you pick the right players. A team with Allen, McCaffrey, and __Puka Nacua__ on it last year would have been really tough to beat, even if that team was fielding sub-replacement-level players at all its other positions. But again, if one of those guys missed significant time — or something else unexpected happens — that team would go belly up.

Replace Puka with __Justin Jefferson__ on last year’s team, and you see what can go wrong easily. There is a significant amount of luck involved with this strategy — it’s not hard to figure out which individual players might be worth 15-25% of your budget by themselves, but it’s not up to you to keep them on the field.

If you do this, you will need to look for players *pre*\-breakout, like rookies or second-year players with some bad vibes — remember, Jettas went for a couple of bucks in 2020, while __Ja’Marr Chase__’s value plummeted after a bad preseason in 2021. You can also choose to buy camp hype on a guy like Puka in 2023. Take advantage of the unknown — you can see that I took some shots on rookie receivers on this team.

On the side of pure pleasure (and after all, we’re trying to have fun here), loading up on stars early in your draft and waiting until the end of your draft before you can even consider bidding on more players is not the best of experiences. __Tom Brolley__, __Graham Barfield__, and I have literally been in a league in which someone who went Stars-N-Scrubs *fell asleep during the draft*.

I would not recommend sacrificing depth for across-the-board star power. __This strategy is not for me, personally, but if you’re trying to take down a big pot, you could rationalize it to yourself by saying, “Look, I want to be first, not seventh. There’s no difference between finishing seventh and last.”__ And if you acknowledge that you need luck to pull this off, the dice roll could be worth it.
